input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. This study compares a polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane for the separation of water from isopropanol, and reports flux, separation factor and stability together for each membrane. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1); the separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless. The feed was 85 wt% isopropanol in water, at 60 °C. The polymer membrane gave a flux of 2.4 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 180, and its flux fell 7% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1.3 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 420, and its flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. The comparison is essentially a trade between throughput and selectivity: the polymer membrane passes more mass per unit area, while the zeolite membrane separates more sharply and holds its flux. For a duty set by the purity of the permeate, the zeolite membrane's selectivity carries the decision; for a duty set by membrane area, the polymer membrane's flux does, at the cost of a declining rate over the run. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the pairing matters here, because the polymer membrane's flux advantage is measured on a declining quantity. The comparison rests on one feed composition, and no test ran beyond 500 h, so neither membrane's behaviour at other compositions or over longer service is established by these results.
